a b s t r a c t
The current strategy of electrocatalytic CO2 reduction reaction (eCO2RR) to generate useful chemicals and hydrocarbons is supposed to effectively mitigate the greenhouse effect. The practical application for eCO2RR in aqueous solutions, however, still was encumbered by its high overpotential, low activity and poor selectivity due to CO2 mass transfer and intermediate stability. Electrocatalytic materials with reduced overpotential and high efficiency and selectivity are exploited for further development. Herein, Ag+ and Cu2+ precursors were co-reduced to generate Ag-Cu bimetallic aerogel after further freeze drying. Compared with Ag100 aerogel, the optimal Ag88Cu12 can effectively decrease overpotential, improve selectivity and current density, and keep electrochemical stability. At 0.89 V vs. RHE, the Faraday efficiency reached 89.40% and the CO partial current density of 5.86 mA cm 2 was obtained. The intrinsic property of metal aerogel (hydrophobic, hierarchical porous structure, conductivity), presence of rich grain boundaries and geometric effect and the introduction of Cu leading to improvement of adsorption between the catalyst and the *COOH intermediate in Ag88Cu12, contribute to the enhanced performance. Furthermore, the strategy of constructing metal aerogel will improve metal catalyst performance towards eCO2RR and pave way for further industrial applications.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
The economic and social development has caused greenhouse effect by the constantly increasing emission of carbon dioxide (CO2), which has an inevitable impact on nature and human living [1–4]. To duel crisis, many researches have been carried out to alleviate the overemission of CO2, and numerous neoteric CO2 conversion systems have been implemented to realize the high-added value of CO2. Electrochemical reduction of CO2, which can be conducted at room temperature with simple equipment, can work as potential solution for curbing the coming environmental danger. Especially, the conversion of relatively low-cost renewable energy (such as wind, solar, and tidal energy) into electrical energy is the primary prerequisite for the advancement of eCO2RR. However, eCO2RR in aqueous solution faced the predicament of sluggish kinetics, high overpotential, low activity and selectivity, which has always hindered the prompt conversion of CO2 to high-value products[5–7]. To solve the problems and achieve the commercial application of eCO2RR, measures such as reforming the flow cell, designing the catalyst, and replacing the electrolyte have been carried out[8–9]. Among them, exploiting catalysts that can reduce the overpotential and boost activity and selectivity is indispensable.
CO, as one of eCO2RR products, is an allimportant organic raw material used to produce methanol and other chemicals in the chemical industry. CO2 is converted into CO in aqueous electrolyte, as shown in equation (1) - (4)[10].
CO2 + e + * ! *CO2 ð1Þ
*CO2 +H + aq !*COOH ð2Þ
*COOH +H + aq+ e !*CO + H2O ð3Þ
*CO ! CO + * ð4Þ Where the meaning of * is the vacant catalytically active site.
According to Hori’s result, Au and Ag were the optimal metal electrode materials for the electrocatalytic CO2 reduction to CO as the main product in aqueous solutions, due to the existence of weak bond between Ag/Au and *CO intermediates making it highly selective to CO during eCO2RR[11]. Ag has greater abundance and lower cost than gold, and it has received more concerns[12]. The desorption thermodynamic potential energy of *CO upon Ag is calculated to be or reported less than zero, and *CO cannot be reduced continuously [13] thus leading to the final product of CO, which also has a good inhibitory effect on hydrogen evolution reaction (HER)[14–15]. To further boost its selectivity and reduce costs, doping with p-block transition metal atoms to form bimetallic catalysts is inspiring. It will not only destroy the binding energy relationship between *COOH as well as *CO and the metal, leading to easy desorption of *CO due to the enhanced stability of the *COOH, but also reduce the initial potential for CO formation on Ag[12–18]. Kottakkat[15] used operando Raman to find that the position of the intramolecular CO band over the Ag-Cu foam moved to a positive potential, indicating that CO was more likely to desorb on the surface of Ag-Cu, which improved the activity of eCO2RR towards CO. Therefore, combining Cu with Ag can save costs, as well further improve its activity and application potential.
Ag-Cu bimetals have been extensively exploring, including their synergistic effects[19] distribution and proportion of atoms, and surface copper structure[20]. However, the different combination of atomic distribution and electronic configuration of active sites lead to the change of binding energy relationship between *COOH as well as *CO and the metal[21–24]. Hoang
[22] electrodeposited Ag and Cu on carbon paper and detected that the presence of silver can help to achieve high selectivity for ethylene and ethanol at low potentials. Lee[24] prepared disparate mixing modes of Ag and Cu by electrodeposition in different solutions, which could adjust the selectivity of ethanol. Increasing the specific surface area to provide more active sites for the reaction and combining with the synergy between the Ag-Cu can also greatly improve the performance of electrocatalytic CO2RR to CO. Zhang et al.[25] carried out anodization/dealloying of alloy foils containing Ag and Cu to obtain a porous structure of Ag-Cu bimetallic electrocatalysts. The sponge-like (Ag91Cu9) morphology was conducive to the exposure of active sites as well as the adsorption of CO2, and 80.6% of FECO was calculated in eCO2RR. Urbain[18] used electrodeposition to prepare Ag-Cu foam on the copper bubble template, and benefited from the morphological advantages to obtain high FECO of 95.7% at 0.8 VRHE. Hence, constructing the Ag/Cu porous structure catalyst is favorable for the formation of CO. Nonetheless, deep understanding of the catalytic mechanism between porous structure and performance is ongoing.
Aerogel is unique solid material, consisting of interconnected three-dimensional solid network and a large number of air-filled pores. It has the characteristics of low density, hydrophobicity, high specific surface area and stability[26] which has been widely applied in the field of sorption, catalysis, supercapacitance[27–29] et al. Metal skeleton aerogel has excellent electronic conductivity (helping to increase the charge transfer rate), large internal specific surface area (increasing the number of active sites) and high porosity (increasing the mass transfer rate), and has potential research in the field of electrocatalytic reduction of CO2 and application prospects’[30]. However, the morphological characteristics of pure metal aerogels reported so far are mainly based on precious metals (Pd, Pt, and Au), which can stand up corrosion and oxidation in humid air and had been widely applied in many fields, such as oxygen reduction reaction[31] methanol oxidation reaction[32] and the like. For better capacity, bimetallic aerogel has been under consideration. Han et al. developed Pd@Cu bimetallic aerogel for electrocatalytic CO2 conversion. The obtained series of PdxCuy aerogels could electrocatalyze CO2 to CH3OH with excellent activity, and the high-porosity, self-supporting network of the material facilitated the exposure of electrochemical active centers, good reaction channels and the synergistic effect of Pd and Cu[33]. Gong et al.[34] synthesized AuCu aerogel, and investigated its eCO2RR both from experiment and theory. The grain boundaries between AuCu porous structure were supposed to concentrate and activate CO2, and enhance its final catalytic efficiency. As to bimetallic aerogel, role of different metal and their constitute influence, however, still remain open debate.
We, herein, describe the synthesis of Ag-Cu bimetallic aerogel via sol-gel, and freeze drying procedure based on our former experience[35–36], and test its performance of electrocatalyzing eCO2RR to CO conversion. The structure and morphology of the catalyst, as well as the electrocatalytic CO2 performance have been explored, and a low overpotential, high activity and selectivity catalyst has been achieved. There are three concerns: (1) Ag-Cu bimetallic aerogel exhibits rich grain boundaries enhancing the adsorption of CO2. (2) Ag-Cu bimetallic aerogel is composed of nanoparticles connected by ligaments with a porous network structure, which not only contributes to mass transfer but also increases the electrochemically active surface area (ECSA) to promote eCO2RR. (3) The geometric effect in Ag-Cu bimetallic aerogel leads to improvement of adsorption between the catalyst and the *COOH intermediate, helps to further stabilize the *COOH intermediate, and increases the Faraday efficiency of CO.

sections.heading: 2.1. Preparation of AgxCuy bimetallic aerogel
sections.text: The AgxCuy bimetallic aerogel was prepared by simultaneously reducing Ag nitrate and copper nitrate with potassium borohydride in an aqueous solution at room temperature. As to Ag88Cu12 aerogel, 15 mL 0.1 M KBH4 was added in 5 mL 0.1 M AgNO3. The solution turned from colorless to black instantly. Then 13.6 mL 5 mM Cu(NO3)2 3H2O aqueous solution was added into the above solution. The mixed liquid in the beaker was shaken quickly for two minutes, and let it stand for 8 h. The resulted black hydrogel was washed five times with deionized water to remove residual impurities in the sample. Then the sample was frozen in the refrigerator and freeze-dried to obtain the Ag88Cu12 bimetal aerogel. Similar to the above method, Ag100 was prepared without Cu2+, and Ag50Cu50 was obtained by controlling the equal molar ratio of Ag to Cu.

sections.heading: 2.2. Electrochemical test
sections.text:
Standard three-electrode H-type electrolytic cell was used in the electrochemical test with the catalyst-loaded carbon paper as the working electrode, Ag/AgCl (saturated with 3.5 M KCl) as the reference electrode, the platinum electrode as the counter electrode. CO2 saturated 0.1 M NaHCO3 (pH = 6.8) was used as the electrolyte, while the two electrode chambers were separated by Nafion-117 ion exchange membrane. 100 lL of the solution was dropped onto carbon paper (0.5 cm2 on one side), and dried overnight at room temperature to obtain working electrode with load of 1 mg cm 2, and then its catalytic performance was tested. Before the test, the electrolyte was continuously ventilated with CO2 gas for more than 30 min to remove all oxygen in the electrolyte, and the CO2 gas flow rate was controlled to 15 sccm. The LSV scan rate was 20 mV s 1, and the electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) was performed at a frequency of 100000 Hz (high) to 1 Hz (low). The products were analyzed in real time by chronoamperometry and on-line gas chromatograph. The duration of each potential was 1 h.
All potentials were relative to the reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE), and the conversion formula was as follows:

sections.heading: 3.1. Synthesis and characterization of catalysts
sections.text:
Typical bimetallic aerogel is prepared by co-reduction using AgNO3 and Cu(NO3)2 3H2O as precursors and KBH4 as reducing agent. The synthesis schematic diagram is shown in Fig. 1a. First, KBH4 is added into AgNO3, and the solution quickly turns black. After addition of Cu(NO3)2, the hydrogel is obtained by standing for 8 h, washed with water in depth and then dried by a freeze dryer to acquire bimetallic aerogel. Fig. 1b-d are scanning electron microscope (SEM) images of Ag100, Ag88Cu12 and Ag50Cu50, showing analogical porous structure, which indicates aerogel structure is not affected by metal ratio and can be universally feasible. The formation of these pores maybe caused by the large amount of overflowing H2 generated while reducing Ag+ and Cu2+ by KBH4. The three-dimensional porous network structure is the most important feature of aerogel materials[38] suggesting the successful preparation of our Ag-Cu bimetallic aerogel. Compared with onedimensional and two-dimensional materials, aerogel has unique advantages in catalysis. The large number of pores in Ag88Cu12 can supply more reaction sites for eCO2RR, and provide transfer channels for unreacted CO2 and generated CO to facilitate the diffusion of gas molecules, which favors its high activity and selectivity. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) further illustrates the successful synthesis of aerogel materials. Aerogel has three types of linkage: (1) bridge, applying to that the average size of the particle joint is smaller than the particle diameter, (2) ligament (size equal to the particle diameter) and (3) island (size larger than particle diameter)[39]. It is confirmed from Fig. 1e that Ag88Cu12 aerogel is composed of nanoparticles connected by ligaments with a porous network structure. As to the high-resolution TEM (Fig. 1f), it can be seen that a large number of grain boundaries are detected in the bimetallic aerogel. The lattice d-spacing of 0.232 nm corresponds to the face-centered-cubic structure of Ag(111)[40] which is further confirmed by the X-ray diffraction pattern (Fig. 2a), and the lattice d-spacing of 0.208 nm corresponds to the Cu(111)[38] (insert of Fig. 1f). STEM high-angle annular dark field-energy dispersive X-ray spectrometer (HAADF-EDX) mapping pictures show that the distribution of Ag and Cu is uniform (Fig. 1g, Fig. S1). The value of BET specific surface area, pore volume and pore size of the bimetallic aerogel catalyst tested by liquid N2 adsorptiondesorption experiment can be seen in the Table S1. The BET surface area and pore size of Ag100, Ag88Cu12, and Ag50Cu50 are 3.04, 8.29, 9.25 m2 g 1 and 4.86, 5.49, 5.12 nm, respectively. Their nitrogen adsorption and desorption curves and pore size distribution are shown in Fig. S2.
In order to understand the crystal structure of AgxCuy bimetallic aerogel, we used X-ray diffraction (XRD) to perform qualitative analysis. Fig. 2a illustrated the XRD pattern of three aerogel materials. It can be seen that Ag100, Ag88Cu12, and Ag50Cu50 all maintain high crystallinity, and there are four diffraction peaks at 2h values of 38.20 , 44.40 , 64.60 , 77.60 , corresponding to the (111), (200), (220) and (311) crystal planes of the Ag face-centered cubic structure (JCPDS87-0718), respectively. It is worth noting that the characteristic peaks of Cu are not detected in Ag88Cu12, and no obvious
shift in the position of the diffraction peaks compared with pure Ag materials. However, with the increase of Cu element, the (111), (200), (220) and (311) crystal plane diffraction peaks of Cu2O in Ag50Cu50 at 36.44 , 42.33 , 61.41 and 73.56 (JCPDS78-2076) were observed, respectively. The result reflected that Cu with low content in Ag88Cu12 was highly dispersed, further confirming that the aerogel material is bimetallic structure rather than alloy [15,21]. Although there was no characteristic diffraction peak of Cu in the XRD spectrum of Ag88Cu12, the even dispersion of Cu in the TEM-EDX element mapping (Fig. 1g) further proved the successful synthesis of bimetallic aerogel. Compared with Ag50Cu50, it can be directly seen from Fig. 2a that the diffraction peaks of Ag100 and Ag88Cu12 are narrower, indicating that they have larger crystal grains and higher crystallinity.
X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was used to further understand the chemical composition and valence band structure of the sample. Figure S3 is the XPS survey spectrum of Ag100, Ag88Cu12 and Ag50Cu50, showing that the characteristic peak of Cu 2p orbital was detected in Ag88Cu12 and Ag50Cu50, which also indicates that the Cu element has been successfully introduced. The high-resolution spectrum (Fig. 2b) shows that the Ag 3d3/2 and Ag 3d5/2 orbitals of Ag100 (374.09 eV and 368.16 eV), Ag88Cu12 (373.97 eV and 367.97 eV) and Ag50Cu50 (373.91 eV and 368.01 eV), respectively. However, all Ag peaks of Ag88Cu12 and Ag50Cu50 skewed slightly towards the direction of decreased binding energy. This phenomenon is attributed to the change of the electronic structure of Ag atoms by the introduction of Cu, which subsequently caused the changes of XPS peak position[16,40].
Fig. 2c shows that the peaks located at 953.17 eV and 932.28 eV are attributed to (Cu0/Cu+) of Ag88Cu12. The bands existing at 934.89 eV and 955.44 eV prove the presence of Cu2+. It should be noted that in addition to the characteristic peak of Cu 2p, there are also two satellite peaks[25,41] corresponding to Cu (Ⅱ) at 941.69 eV, 944.04 eV, and 962.66 eV, indicating the presence of Cu2+ on the surface of Ag88Cu12. This is because the Cu atoms on the surface are easily oxidized when the sample is transferred in the air[34] which corresponds to the greater O 1 s signal intensity of Ag88Cu12 in Fig. S3. Similarly, there is an O 1 s signal in the XPS total spectrum of Ag100. Since Fig. 2b shows that the Ag is metallic state, the O 1 s signal may be due to the presence of adsorbed oxygen on the sample surface.

sections.heading: 3.2. Electrochemical CO2RR of Ag-Cu bimetallic aerogel
sections.text:
In order to verify the activity for eCO2RR, Ag100, Ag88Cu12, and Ag50Cu50 were loaded on hydrophobic carbon paper for electrochemical measurement in CO2-saturated 0.1 M NaHCO3, using the H-type standard three-electrode system (Fig. S4). The contact angles of the working electrode of Ag100, Ag88Cu12, and Ag50Cu50 were 129.9 , 133.0 and 131.8 (inset of Fig. 1b-d), respectively, and hydrophobic/aerophilic interface facilitates the contact between the catalyst and protons, inhibiting the progress of HER while enhancing the CO2 concentration on the electrode surface [42]. For the purpose of guaranteeing the same quality of the catalyst, we controlled the catalyst loading of 1 mg cm 2. Before the electrochemical test, we performed a multi-circle CV scan on the
working electrode. As to Ag88Cu12 and Ag50Cu50, there were two obvious reduction peaks near 0 V and 0.5 V (Fig. S5), corresponding to the oxidation state of Cu appeared in the XPS pattern. The peaks will disappear after multiscan, indicating that it is elemental copper not oxidized copper participating eCO2RR.
The linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) curves show that the initial potentials of Ag100, Ag88Cu12, and Ag50Cu50 are obtained at 0.59 V, 0.44 V, 0.36 V, respectively. Compared with Ag100, the initial potential of Ag-Cu bimetallic aerogel has moved somewhat towards positive direction (Fig. 3a). Ag88Cu12 obtains total current density of 9.17 mA cm 2 at 1.0 V, which is approximately 2.58 times higher than that of Ag100 ( 3.56 mA cm 2). Compared with Ag50Cu50 ( 9.63 mA cm 2), the current density is not much different, yet all the AgxCuy bimetallic aerogels show a larger current density than the pure Ag aerogel.
The eCO2RR product was detected by gas chromatography. The chronocurrent curve is shown in Fig. S6. The FECO of Ag100 can reach more than 48% at a low potential of 0.69 V, accompanied by severe competitive hydrogen evolution reaction (HER). As the potential negative shift, FECO of Ag100 gradually increases. The maximum FECO of 83.76% was obtained at 0.99 V, showing that the relatively low overpotential is not enough to drive eCO2RR to compete with HER[25]. Furthermore, due to the weak bond between Ag and the *CO intermediate, *CO cannot be continu-
ously reduced[13] causing a mass of *CO desorption and releasing considerable CO[43]. However, when the potential becomes more negative, the Faraday efficiency of H2 begins to increase (Fig. S7). The reason for the increase in FEH2 maybe that the low concentration of CO2 cannot make full use of the electrons provided under high potential. As to bimetal aerogel, the FECO value of Ag88Cu12 is mostly greater than that of Ag100, and reaches the maximum value of 89.40% at 0.89 V. The FID and TCD curves of the individual signal peaks of CO and H2 under Ag88Cu12 are shown in Fig. S8. Compared with Ag100 at 0.89 V, the FECO of Ag88Cu12 is increased by 10%. As for Ag50Cu50, it only reached the maximum FECO of 73.98% at 0.99 V (Fig. 3c). Fig. 3d is the partial current density of CO for the three catalysts towards eCO2RR, showing that Ag88Cu12 exhibits the largest CO partial current density. The jCO of Ag88Cu12 is 5.86 mA cm 2 at 0.89 V, and it is 4.61 and 1.71 times higher than that of Ag100 and Ag50Cu50, respectively. From LSV and CO partial current density, we conclude that Ag-Cu bimetallic aerogel has greatly improved eCO2RR activity compared with pure Ag metallic aerogel. The energy efficiency of aerogel catalysts for CO is calculated at different potential. Ag88Cu12 showed a maximum EECO value of ~ 56.3% under 0.89 V vs. RHE among all tested samples (Fig. 3e). The performance of Ag88Cu12 is better than most of the reported silvercopper bimetallic catalysts, (Fig. 3f and detailed analysis in Table S2 [15,19,25,41,43–47]).

sections.heading: 3.3. Intrinsic activity of Ag-Cu bimetallic aerogel towards eCO2RR
sections.text: In view of the fact that the excellent electrocatalytic activity of Ag-Cu bimetallic aerogel catalyst for eCO2RR compared with pure silver aerogel, we seek to study the structure-activity relationship of Ag-Cu bimetallic aerogel. Working electrodes loaded with Ag-Cu bimetallic aerogel (1 mg cm 2) and pure silver aerogel (1 mg cm 2) are used to study the electrochemically active surface area (ECSA) of Ag-Cu bimetallic aerogel in the non-Faraday current range. Figure S9 is their respective cyclic voltammetry curves (CV), and the scan rate varies from 20 mV s 1 to 100 mV s 1. The Cdl (doublelayer capacitance) value of Ag-Cu bimetallic aerogel and pure silver aerogel is proportional to ECSA, calculated to be 0.8 mF cm 2 (Ag100), 3.84 mF cm 2 (Ag88Cu12) and 3.73 mF cm 2 (Ag50Cu50) (Fig. 3b). It is worth noting that the ECSA value of Ag-Cu bimetallic aerogel is much greater than that of pure silver aerogel, and Ag88Cu12 has the highest ECSA value among all samples, indicating that it has more active sites for eCO2RR. We also conducted an Electrochemical Impedance Spectroscopy (EIS) experiment to study the electron transfer rate of Ag-Cu bimetallic aerogel catalysts in CO2-saturated 0.1 M NaHCO3 electrolyte as shown in Fig. S10. The semicircle size of Ag88Cu12 is smaller than that of Ag100 and Ag50Cu50, indicating that Ag88Cu12 has the fastest charge transfer process.

sections.heading: 3.4. Reaction mechanism
sections.text:
The reaction mechanism of aerogel in the process of eCO2RR reduction was explored. We calculated the Tafel slopes of three aerogels to reflect the electron transfer kinetics in the eCO2RR process (Fig. 4a). The Tafel slope of Ag100 is close to 118 mV dec 1, indicating that the rate-determining step is one electron transfer step (CO2 + e + * ? *CO2 ) that produces the key intermediate *CO2 [48]. The Tafel slope of Ag88Cu12 is close to 59 mV dec 1, indicating that Ag88Cu12 has a rapid initial electron transfer process, and the subsequent electron transfer step (*COOH +
Hþaq + e ? *CO + H2O) is the rate-determining step[49]. A large number of grain boundaries in bimetallic aerogels can be seen in HRTEM (Fig. 1f). We suggest that the existence of grain boundaries is difficult for electron to travel across, which leads to a large accumulation of electrons to form an electric field to attract cations in the electrolyte and improve the concentration of CO2 on the electrode surface[34]. Furthermore, eCO2RR is a surface reaction, and its catalytic activity largely depends on the specific surface area, which increases the contact between the reactants and the active center[33–34]. Hence, Ag-Cu bimetallic aerogel with larger specific surface area exhibit potential activity than that of pure Ag aerogel.
Stabilizing the *CO2 intermediate and converting to *COOH can help the eCO2RR process to proceed efficiently. In order to determine the binding energy strength between the intermediate and the catalyst, cyclic voltammetry was carried out in N2-saturated 0.1 M NaOH aqueous solution using OH to replace CO2 . The overpotential of OH adsorption can be used to evaluate the bonding strength of intermediates with catalyst, and small overpotential means a strong bond between the intermediate and the catalyst [48,50]. Fig. 4b shows the voltammograms of OH adsorption and desorption peaks in 0.1 M NaOH. In the experiment, the scanning range is 0.3 V ~ 0.6 V (vs. Ag/AgCl), and the scanning rate is 10 mV s 1. The surface adsorption overpotential of OH is the lowest for Ag88Cu12, which indicates that it possesses greater adsorption strength of OH , and hence the stronger bond between Ag88Cu12 and CO2 . Rapid initial electron transfer and more effective fixation of CO2 intermediate can promote the process of eCO2RR, demonstrating the superiority of Ag88Cu12 in reducing CO2 to CO.
Since the configuration of the active site have a great impact on the binding strength of the intermediate, geometric effects play an important role in determining the catalytic activity. Seen from TEM-EDX (Fig. 1g), the bimetallic aerogel has a uniform phase, assuming that the composition of the two elements is evenly distributed throughout the aerogel. The Cu atom is adjacent to the Ag-C primary bond. At this position, it can form a bond with the
oxygen end of *COOH, which can further stabilize *COOH[51]. Hence, the geometric effect in bimetallic aerogels helps to enhance the selectivity of CO.
The reaction process is shown in Fig. 5. The accumulation of electrons in the grain boundaries results in CO2 enrichment and subsequent adsorption and activation. CO2 is converted to*CO2 by obtaining one electron and then *COOH by obtaining one H+
on the catalyst surface. Then, after dehydration, *CO is obtained and finally the intermediate desorption produces CO as a product.

sections.heading: 3.5. Stability test
sections.text:
In order to further assess the eCO2RR performance of Ag88Cu12, we conducted a stability test for up to 8 h at 0.89 V, as shown in Fig. S11. The gas phase products were fed into the gas chromatograph every 30 min, and their respective Faraday efficiencies were calculated according to the percentages of H2 and CO gas concentrations calculated from the TCD and FID curves. It can be seen that the current density remains relatively stable without too much fluctuation, FECO can be maintained above 85%, and the hydrogen evolution reaction is well suppressed during the whole process, indicating that the Ag88Cu12 bimetallic aerogel catalyst can remain stable activity during long-term electrolysis. It should be noted that in order to avoid salt precipitation caused by oxygen evolution at the anode, our stability test is divided into two parts. Every four hours, the electrolyte is replaced. We ensure
that the working electrode and electrolyte in the cathode chamber remain unchanged. Because of this, the FECO after 4.5 h has a significant decrease, but the FECO in the two parts shows the same trend.
Fig. 6(a-c) shows the aerogel electrode material after reaction still maintains continuous 3D porous structure, which indicates that the prepared metal aerogel can maintain outstanding structural stability. The TEM image also proves this. The TEM image still shows abundant grain boundaries, but it can be seen that there is a layer of coating on the outer surface of the aerogel which is resulted from the Nafion solution used in the electrode preparation process. We directly carried out the XRD test of the working electrode after the reaction (Fig. 6d), and used blank carbon paper (the substrate of the working electrode) as a parameter. It can be observed that the crystal face of the metal aerogel is not changed during the electrolysis process, which is similar with that before the electrochemical test (Fig. 2a), proving the superior structural stability. Since the oxidized copper was reduced during the electrolysis process, it can be observed from Fig. 6f that only elemental copper is present in the Cu 2p orbital. The peaks at 374.35 eV and 368.35 eV corresponding to the Ag 3d3/2 and Ag 3d5/2 orbitals after the reaction of Ag88Cu12 (Fig. 6e), respectively, which are positively shifted by 0.38 eV compared to sample before the reaction. This may be due to changes in the photoelectrons of silver caused by the change in the valence state of copper.

sections.heading: 4. Conclusions
sections.text:
In summary, we have co-reduced metal precursor to prepare Ag-Cu bimetallic aerogels that can efficiently electrocatalyze CO2RR. The porous structure of Ag88Cu12 bimetallic aerogel facilitates the mass transfer efficiency so that CO2 can contact more catalytically active centers. Moreover, the rich grain boundaries in the bimetal Ag88Cu12 assist CO2 adsorption on the electrode surface, so the contact of CO2 with the surface of the catalyst is increased, and the problem of low solubility of CO2 in the aqueous solution is alleviated. Meanwhile, the introduction of a small amount of copper reduces the reaction overpotential, increases stability of *COOH, and improves the selectivity of CO. At 0.89 V, Ag88Cu12 achieves an excellent Faraday efficiency of 89.40% with a CO local current density of 5.86 mA cm 2, which is significantly improved compared with Ag100. This work uses one-step reduction method to prepare a novel bimetallic aerogel material, and this approach avoids the excessive pursuit to the morphology of the catalyst, and improves the catalytic efficiency by introducing copper, which is conducive to the large-scale application of the catalyst and provides a reasonable strategy to prepare other multimetal aerogels for eCO2RR or other areas.
